newsitem.title: USA: USDA seen raising US corn/soybean output estimates.
newsitem.headline: USDA seen raising US corn/soybean output estimates.

text.p: Small upward revisions to both U.S. corn and soybean production estimates are expected to be made by the U.S. Department of Agriculture on Friday following promising early yields, analysts said.
But there are already some signs that yields for later planted crops will be less impressive, particularly on corn.
"The last two days I'm beginning to hear (corn) test weights off and yields off. This was bound to happen with the extensive spread of planting dates," said Chicago Corp analyst Dave Armstrong.
"I haven't heard of it yet on the beans but I think it will be the case," Armstrong added.
A Reuter survey of analysts produced an average estimate for U.S. corn production of 8.951 billion bushels, up from USDA's September projection of 8.804 billion.
The average forecast for U.S. soybean production was 2.287 billion, versus USDA's September estimate of 2.270 billion.

Analyst Steve Freed, of ADM Investor Services, noted the USDA projection was based on conditions as of October 1 when only a very small proportion of crops had been harvested. Reported corn yields have subsequently begun to decline.
"Now we have entered the next level of harvest, the 10 to 30 percent band, we are still hearing good bean yields but corn yields are coming down," Freed said.

USDA has reported that, as of Sunday, the soybean harvest was 17 percent complete, behind a five-year average of 31 percent. The corn harvest was 14 percent done, also behind the average pace of 24 percent.

"A lot of farmers are worried about (corn) test weights. Last year we had a lot of test weights between 56 and 59 lbs but this year we are hearing weights as low as 53 lbs," Freed of ADM Investor Services said.
Analysts said yields of soybeans may start to drop off shortly as later-planted crops are harvested.
"It is going to be real important how the late season beans come through on yields," said Jerry Gidel, analyst with Dean Witter Reynolds.
"There are all kinds of theories out there -- some good, some bad. Early season yields are good but we have still got plenty of harvest ahead of us," he added.
Doug Hjort, president of Hjort Associates, also said the promising performance of early-planted crops would not necessarily be matched by those soybeans seeded later.

"We're hearing good yields on the beans and people are saying it's better than expected, but what should they have expected? They've been saying all along the early stuff was supposed to be good," Hjort said.
